{"voice_profile":"Light, brisk comic-thriller narration. The narrator is close to Tommy and Tuppence and mildly ironic about them, with mock-formal phrasing such as "Mr. Beresford obliged" and "Nobody did, which was the great thing." Most of the effect comes through dialogue. The two leads trade slangy banter ("old thing", "old bean", "Don't be a wretch") and deflate each other's vanity. They parody detective fiction and formal speech: plans of campaign, "Proceed, O Sherlock!", "a literary flavour". Tuppence frankly loves money; Tommy is slow, practical and deadpan. Mr. Carter speaks in a tired, reflective monotone of hedged exposition. Julius uses American idiom ("Put me wise", "Sure thing", "I guess") and gets things done by forceful, moneyed impatience. Menace arrives suddenly in a short closing line after comedy. The text uses double hyphens for breaks and interruptions, four-hyphen trailing-offs, ellipses, and underscore emphasis.","book_context":"The plot runs as a chain of small coincidences. Tommy's overheard name leads to Whittington, the advertisement brings Carter and Julius, and the survivor list yields Rita. Each lead opens the next, and Mr. Brown repeatedly strikes just ahead of them. Chapters IV–VII set up the governing premises: the Danvers/Lusitania backstory, the draft treaty, and the Brown method. That method means a nondescript, overlooked figure behind someone else, a common name, and the unanswerable 'one of us'. These chapters also introduce Julius, with his genealogy and the single photograph, and tie Rita to the name Marguerite. Later revelations depend on all of this: the identity of Mr. Brown, the false Jane at Manchester, the photograph in Julius's drawer, Annette's 'Marguerite' cry, and the 29th. unnoticed, and that the elusive Mr. Brown has escaped us once more.","purpose":"The core Brown method, and the clue that pays off much later."},{"paragraph":94,"text":"That is the invariable description of Mr. Brown!","purpose":"Carter's weary punchline linking the ordinary clerk to Brown."},{"paragraph":102,"text":"And _I_‘ll look after _you_","purpose":"Tuppence's retort to Tommy's 'manly assertion'; characteristic banter with emphasis."},{"paragraph":103,"text":"The curious

Carter answers 'No names, please'; the house is lent by his cousin, so the work is unofficial. Tuppence tells the whole story.","Carter's offer: work for him unofficially, expenses paid, a moderate salary ('screw'), and the task 'Find Jane Finn'.","The Danvers story in causal order: the draft treaty drawn up in neutral America in 1915; Danvers carries it on the Lusitania in an oilskin packet; his body is found but the packet is missing; he was seen speaking to a young American girl; he was possibly shadowed. She is Jane Finn, an orphan pupil teacher going to a Paris hospital, traced across Ireland and then lost. The treaty went unused, so it was assumed destroyed.","Why it matters now: the treaty was once a weapon for Britain and is now a weapon against it. It implicates statesmen and could serve Labour as a party cry, but the real danger is Bolshevist gold and the unknown man behind them, 'Mr. Brown'. Keep Carter's hedges ('I do not believe in its likelihood myself', 'in my opinion').","Brown's profile: believed English, not German; aims probably at supreme power; always plays a secondary part, behind a nonentity. They are seeking information about Jane from Carter's side. Carter's hypothesis of a false Jane in Paris, and Tuppence realizing that was the plan for her.
